comment: Hand-labelled real-machine evaluation set for AppTrace. Ground truth here was reviewed by a human against the machine's own evidence (uninstall registry, directory contents, executable metadata, and the installer path itself) - it was NOT generated from the engine's output. Application identities and install locations were taken from samples/real-machine-scan.json so the engine sees what a real run sees. Cases whose ground truth could not be justified are marked "uncertain" and are reported separately instead of being counted as metrics; they must be resolved by a human, not guessed. See docs/EVALUATION.md.

cases.description: NVIDIA App recommendation store named after a game.
cases.reasoning: The path is inside NVIDIA App's own NvBackend tree, which the engine's own scan shows is NVIDIA App storage. 'cities_skylines' names the subject of a stored recommendation, not the writer. Verified on disk: the NVIDIA app directory exists and contains NVIDIA App.exe (CompanyName 'NVIDIA Corporation'). Labelled as 'no owner' because the creditable owner is NVIDIA App and the game does not own these bytes; the V2 relationship model (Task 06) is what will express 'owned by NVIDIA App, related to Cities: Skylines'.

cases.description: Electron framework directory inside DaVinci Resolve, claimed by Git.
cases.reasoning: The only executable is electron.exe, whose version resource is ProductName 'Electron', CompanyName 'GitHub, Inc.'. The engine matched Git because 'git' is a substring of 'githubinc' - a spurious match with no relation to Git. The path lies inside DaVinci Resolve's install tree. This is a real, reproducible instance of the substring-matching defect described in docs/ATTRIBUTION_ENGINE_V2.md section A.3.

cases.description: Publisher-level directory declared as one product's install location.
cases.reasoning: The directory is named after the publisher, not a product. Its subdirectory is the actual product ('Oxford Discover 1'), which is where the product's own data lives. Crediting the whole publisher namespace to one of its products is the pattern docs/ATTRIBUTION_ENGINE_V2.md calls a vendor-namespace leak. Confidence is medium rather than high because the product's uninstaller does sit directly in this directory.

cases.description: Steam game soundtrack directory inside a game install.
cases.reasoning: The path is inside steamapps/common/Cities_Skylines, so these bytes belong to that game's installation. Labelled as correct ownership rather than a false positive. Confidence is medium because the game was discovered only by name (it has no install location in the uninstall registry).

cases.description: Install location whose folder is named after the product.
cases.reasoning: Declared as the install location by the product itself, and verified on disk: new_quark.exe, quark_proxy.exe and new_quark_proxy.exe all report ProductName 'Quark'. The folder name, the registry claim and the executable metadata all agree.

cases.description: Registry-declared install location inside a shared vendor namespace.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location and an exact product-name folder, with six Adobe products installed so the vendor namespace cannot simply absorb it. Independently verified: the engine's scan attributes this exact directory to this product with DeclaredInstallLocation evidence.

cases.description: Microsoft Edge application directory.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location of Microsoft Edge. EdgeWebView2 Runtime is a sibling Microsoft product with a different declared location, so this case also checks that two Microsoft products are told apart.

cases.description: Edge WebView2 Runtime directory, sibling of Edge.
cases.reasoning: Separately declared install location for the WebView2 runtime. Pairs with the Edge case to prove the two are not conflated.

cases.description: Install location for a product inside a vendor namespace.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location and an exact product-name folder with a distinctive token.

cases.description: Electron-style install location under LocalAppData\Programs.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location. Two sibling products from one publisher are installed, so the case also checks they are not merged.

cases.description: Second Trae product with its own declared install location.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location of the sibling product. Mirror of the case above.

cases.description: Product directory named with a version suffix.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location plus executable metadata. The version suffix is structure, not identity, and must not prevent the match.

cases.description: Product directory nested under a vendor namespace.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location. Two Tencent products are installed, so the Tencent namespace must resolve to the right product rather than to the vendor.

cases.description: Versioned product directory under a vendor namespace.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location below a version directory. The version segment must not be treated as identity, and the product must still win over its Tencent sibling.

cases.description: Install location named after a game launcher platform.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location and an exact folder match.

cases.description: Install location whose folder lacks the display name's version.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location. Display name carries a version that the folder does not, so normalization must strip it.

cases.description: Install location with a short product-specific token.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location and an exact folder match.

cases.description: Product directory nested under its vendor namespace.
cases.reasoning: Declared install location. The localised display name means the match must come from the registry path, not the display name.

cases.description: Program Files install directory for an app that stores data in AppData.
cases.reasoning: Exact product-name folder. OneDrive declares no install location, so this case checks that a correct owner is still found without registry help, and that the Microsoft namespace does not hand it to Edge.

cases.description: Per-user data directory for a distinctively named product.
cases.reasoning: Full name coverage with a distinctive brand token, and Vivaldi's declared install location sits directly beneath this path. Must remain a correct owner even if V2 lowers the confidence.

cases.description: Per-user data inside a shared vendor namespace.
cases.reasoning: The leaf names one product inside a namespace shared by two Google products. Coverage is 0.50 and the name is distinctive.

cases.description: Per-user data inside the publisher's own namespace.
cases.reasoning: Distinctive product name inside its publisher namespace, with no competing Kingsoft product installed.

cases.description: Per-user data for Edge, sharing the Microsoft namespace with OneDrive.
cases.reasoning: Leaf names the product within a namespace shared by two Microsoft products. Pairs with the OneDrive case.

cases.description: Per-user data for OneDrive.
cases.reasoning: Mirror of the Edge case; a rule that fixes one must not break the other.

cases.description: Adobe shared plug-ins directory used by several products.
cases.reasoning: A 'Common' plugins directory is by construction shared by every installed Adobe host application. It must never be attributed to one product, and a structural SHARED/AMBIGUOUS answer is correct.

cases.description: npm package-manager cache root.
cases.reasoning: A package-manager cache is not owned by any product's identity; it is shared scratch space for the npm tool the user runs. Node.js Krypton via nvm-windows is an installed toolchain but does not own this directory.

cases.description: Downloaded browser binary under a test tool's cache.
cases.reasoning: This is Playwright's own downloaded Chromium build, not Google Chrome and not an npm dependency of the installed Node toolchain. No installed application declares or owns this path.

cases.description: A scan root itself, which no application owns.
cases.reasoning: A well-known container directory is never an application's storage. Any attribution here would credit a product with other products' data.

cases.description: Application payload subdirectory of a named product.
cases.reasoning: The path is inside Feishu's own tree, so a V2 engine would say Feishu owns the scope. Labelled 'no owner' for the leaf because two applications with the same publisher (Feishu and Lark) are present and neither declares this exact path, so the leaf itself is not independently attributable. Confidence is medium: a human might reasonably say Feishu owns it.

cases.description: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: product directory beneath a publisher directory.
cases.reasoning: Plausibly owned by the product, since the folder names it and the product's uninstaller lives one level up. Not marked certain because the registry declares only the parent publisher directory, so the product's claim to this leaf is inferred rather than sourced. Listed for review.
cases.label: uncertain

cases.description: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: game platform directory declared as a product's install location.
cases.reasoning: Verified on disk to contain FeverGamesLauncher.exe, benchmark.exe and FeverGamesRepair.exe from a game platform, plus two version directories and a downloaded benchmark program. That suggests the directory belongs to the platform rather than to the single product that declares it, but the uninstall entry does nominate it, so the correct V2 answer is genuinely arguable. Listed for review.
cases.label: uncertain

cases.description: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: NVIDIA App program directory.
cases.reasoning: Verified on disk to contain 'NVIDIA App.exe' with CompanyName 'NVIDIA Corporation', and the engine's own Recommended-relation case depends on this tree being NVIDIA App storage. Not marked certain because the path was not emitted as an accounted location by the Phase 0 scan, so it cannot be reconciled against the scan directly. Listed for review.
cases.label: uncertain

cases.description: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: per-user shader cache named after a game.
cases.reasoning: The folder names the game, which is plausible ownership of its own shader cache. Not marked certain because the game's install was not independently confirmed in the scan, and a shader cache can equally be written by a launcher or the GPU driver on the game's behalf. Listed for review.
cases.label: uncertain

cases.description: NEEDS HUMAN REVIEW: product root with no subdirectory evidence.
cases.reasoning: The folder name matches the installed product exactly and no sibling product exists, so attribution looks safe. Not marked certain because the engine reached this conclusion from a name match alone with no registry or executable corroboration, and the underlying directory contents were not inspected. Listed for review.
cases.label: uncertain
